# Cybersecurity concept

The cybersecurity concept, [WP-C-10](../WP-C-10-cybersecurity-goals-and-concept.md), answers the
[TARA](../tara/README.md). For every threat at risk 3 or above, it states a cybersecurity goal: the property to
protect, not the mechanism. It records what is assumed about the world outside the item and which risks are accepted
rather than reduced. It then allocates controls and concept-level requirements to the elements, under ISO/SAE 21434.

This page walks through the concept with its figures. The document is the source of record, and every figure here is
generated from it. It is a defensive concept with no exploitation detail.

**The concept in five lines.**

1. **Eight cybersecurity goals**, CSG-01 to CSG-08. Each covers one or more threat scenarios of the TARA and has a
   proposed assurance level: four at CAL 3 and four at CAL 2. No CAL is claimed as achieved.
2. **Two goals protect every safety goal.** These are the integrity of the panda's safety configuration (CSG-01) and the
   authenticity of its firmware (CSG-02), because the envelope is where an attack and a safety failure converge.
3. **Five claims** record what is not reduced: two risks retained, two shared with comma.ai or suppliers, and one
   avoided by excluding the external compute (E-06).
4. **Sixteen concept-level requirements**, CSR-C-01 to CSR-C-16. At the baseline one is implemented, in the reference
   build only, two are partly done and thirteen are not started. None is verified.
5. **The lead's decisions so far:** remote access, SSH, uploads and developer modes are off by default and opt-in only
   (DQ-020), and updates become signed releases (DQ-075).

## 1. From the threats to the goals

The TARA places its threats on the item. The concept answers each one there.

![WP-C-09 Figure 1-1: the item boundary in the cybersecurity view: each element with the assets it holds, the threat scenarios against them by risk value and the attack paths that enter there](../figures/fig-c09-1-1-cybersecurity-view.svg)

*What the TARA found ([WP-C-09](../WP-C-09-tara.md) Figure 1-1).* The highest risks sit on the openpilot side and on
the panda safety MCU.

| Goal | Protects | Threats (risk) | CAL |
|---|---|---|---|
| CSG-01 | The panda safety configuration: safety mode and parameter | TS-02 (5) | 3 |
| CSG-02 | The panda firmware and its boot chain | TS-03 (5), TS-05 (4) | 3 |
| CSG-03 | Safety-relevant parameters and IPC: actuation, model output, driver monitoring | TS-04 (5), TS-12 (4) | 2 |
| CSG-04 | ML model artefacts at load: no code execution | TS-09 (4) | 2 |
| CSG-05 | Safety-relevant vehicle-CAN messages, received and sent | TS-01 (4), TS-14 (5) | 2 (to be re-derived, OI-8) |
| CSG-06 | Remote and interactive access, minimized and authenticated | TS-07 (4), TS-08 (4), TS-13 (3) | 3 |
| CSG-07 | Software updates, verified end to end | TS-06 (4), TS-10 (4) | 3 |
| CSG-08 | Personal data and the identity key, in transit and at rest | TS-11 (5), TS-07 (4) | 2 |

The CAL follows the risk value and how the threat reaches the item (§3). A remote, network-reachable or fleet-wide
threat to safety gets CAL 3. A threat that needs local or physical access gets CAL 2.

## 2. What is assumed, and what is accepted

**Assumptions on the world outside (§2).** The concept does not claim to secure what is outside the item. It assumes:

- no safety function depends on comma.ai's servers (CA-01);
- the code host and update origin can be compromised, so LionDriver authenticates code itself (CA-02);
- anyone with physical access can reach the vehicle bus (CA-03);
- the network is untrusted (CA-04);
- the owner normally controls the device, and theft is a bounded event (CA-05).

**Claims (§5): risks not reduced to zero, and why that is acceptable.**

| Claim | What is accepted | Type |
|---|---|---|
| CSC-01 | CAN injection with physical access stays at the level of any car with an OBD port | Retain |
| CSC-02 | The security of comma.ai's back end and the network is theirs; no safety function depends on it | Share |
| CSC-03 | Non-repudiation stays at the level of the per-device key | Retain |
| CSC-04 | Off-the-shelf binaries (AGNOS, toolchain wheels) are pinned by hash and monitored, not source-verified | Share |
| CSC-05 | The optional external compute is excluded from the reference configuration | Avoid |

## 3. The concept on the item

![WP-C-10 Figure 6-1: the concept-level cybersecurity requirements CSR-C-01 to CSR-C-16 on the places they are allocated to: the panda safety firmware and the SoC inside the item, the comma.ai back end and the owner, installer and operation outside it, each with its goal, CAL and status](../figures/fig-c10-6-1-concept-view.svg)

*Where each requirement lives (WP-C-10 §6–§7, Figure 6-1).* The panda firmware carries the requirements that protect
the envelope:
- the safety-mode lock, the one requirement implemented, in the reference build only;
- the boot chain, signing and flash protection;
- the CAN checks.

The SoC carries the rest: parameter and IPC integrity, model loading, SSH and remote access, updates and personal data.
A requirement that needs the owner or comma.ai as well, such as update signing or decommissioning, is drawn in each
place it touches.

## 4. What each goal's control stops

![WP-C-10 Figure 7-1: eight cybersecurity goal cards, each with its CAL, the threat scenarios it addresses and their risk, a scene of the threat meeting the goal's control, and its concept-level requirements with their status](../figures/fig-c10-7-1-goal-cards.svg)

*The goal cards (§7.1, Figure 7-1).* Each card shows the threat entering, meeting the goal's control at its element,
and either stopping there or reaching the car. The control is drawn as built. No requirement is verified yet, so no
barrier is solid.

## 5. Where security protects safety

An attacker who reaches the envelope can cause the same hazards a fault can. §8 maps every safety goal to the
cybersecurity goals that keep an attacker from inducing its hazard:

| Safety goal (ASIL) | Protected by |
|---|---|
| SG-01 lateral motion (C) | CSG-01, 02, 03, 05 |
| SG-02 no silent loss of steering (C) | CSG-01…07 |
| SG-03 no unintended acceleration (C) | CSG-01, 02, 03, 05 |
| SG-04 bounded deceleration (B) | CSG-01, 02, 03, 05 |
| SG-05 release on driver action (B) | CSG-01, 02, 03, 05 |
| SG-06 no silent loss of deceleration (C) | CSG-01…07 |
| SG-07 stock PCS preserved (B) | CSG-01, 02, 03, 05 |
| SG-08 driver supervised (A) | CSG-03 |

The [FSC safety view](../fsc/README.md) shows the other side: the envelope carries most of the safety requirements. The
[HATARA](../hatara/README.md) records where a safety measure and a security measure meet.

## 6. Open items

The ones that can change the concept are below; the full list is in WP-C-10.

- **OI-1:** decide the panda signing and boot-chain approach; it fixes the CAL that CSG-01 and CSG-02 can reach.
- **OI-3:** confirm whether personal data and the identity key are encrypted at rest (CSG-08).
- **OI-4:** agree the CAL proposals with the independent assessor.
- **OI-5:** design the signed update (CSG-07). The lead has decided on signed releases (DQ-075).
- **OI-7:** refine CSR-C-01…16 into the detailed requirements of WP-S-07.
- **OI-8:** re-derive the CAL of CSG-05, now that it also covers TS-14 (risk 5).
